paras: The lynching of Charles Pierce took place in Bloomington, McLean County, Illinois, on the night of October 1, 1881, when a crowd of about 5,000 broke into the county jail and hanged Pierce, a prisoner held for horse stealing, from a nearby tree. Earlier that evening Pierce had shot and killed the jailer, Ted Franks. Papers nationwide noted that "best citizens" led the mob, which blamed the courts for failing to punish murder.

Pierce, about 20, was awaiting trial in the jail at the corner of Centre and Market streets for stealing a horse, or a horse and buggy. A Jacksonville, Illinois, dispatch said his real name was Charles Hewlett, of Mount Pleasant, Iowa, and that he had been arrested there that summer with a rig stolen in Bloomington. The town was also angry that the Illinois Supreme Court, in a decision received a day earlier, had reversed the death sentence of Patsy Devine for the 1879 murder of Aaron Goodfellow.

At about 6:30 p.m., as Franks moved him between cells, Pierce seized the jailer's revolver and shot him three times; other prisoners then overpowered him. A crowd gathered at the jail, where men told the Chicago Tribune's correspondent there was "no law against murder" in McLean County. After about an hour men began battering the jail with sledgehammers and timbers, while the sheriff and police fought them at the doors and Senator Fifer and State's Attorney R. B. Porter, promising a trial, were hooted down.

Lieutenant Governor John M. Hamilton telegraphed Governor S. M. Cullom that the mob meant to kill the prisoner "and probably Patsy Devine"; Cullom authorized calling the local military company, but it could not be assembled. Firemen sent to turn water on the crowd withdrew at cries of "Cut the hose."

Inside, an officer pointed out Pierce, who was dragged with a rope to a tree on Market Street near the corner of Centre and Market. Officer Bailey cut the rope once and was nearly killed trying again, after which a man on the branch repeatedly hauled the body up and dropped it as the crowd, women among them, cheered "There's law for you!" The body hung about thirty minutes before the coroner took it, and Devine was not touched, though Goodfellow's father had urged lynching both men.

On October 3 a coroner's jury found that Pierce died by hanging at the hands of a mob whose members were "unknown to the jury." Thousands viewed the wrecked jail and the body the next day, a card on the tree praised "the boys that did it," and the Tribune found no regret over Pierce's death. No report of arrests or prosecutions of the lynchers appears in the coverage.

The Chicago Tribune covered the lynching most fully, printing its correspondent's dispatch on October 2 and again on October 3 under headlines including "ANTI-SUPERSEDEAS" and "Lynch Law Triumphant in a Law-Abiding City in Illinois." Its editorial called mob law repugnant but said Bloomington had "great provocation" from courts given to "quibble," placing responsibility for lynching on courts and lawyers, a theme it repeated in November.

A Chicago summary featuring "best citizens" and cheering women ran on October 3 in the Daily Kennebec Journal, the New-York Tribune and the Washington Evening Star. Shorter items appeared in the Memphis Daily Appeal, the St. Paul Globe, the Austin Weekly Democratic Statesman and weekly crime columns.

Democratic and Southern papers used the case against Northern critics: the Ravenna Democratic Press reprinted a Pittsburgh Post jab at the Tribune for "perpetually shrieking" about the South, and the Bolivar Bulletin wrote that "it is not alone in the South that lynch law prevails." No report stated Pierce's race; the Rock Island Argus called him an "erratic" Iowa horse thief whose stepfather was a bank cashier.

Accounts timed the shooting from 6 to about 6:50 p.m., and two weekly briefs misdated it September 30 or October 4. The jailer also appears as Tad B. and Frederick Franks, and the tree as a maple, a locust or an elm.
